purpose: Golimumab is used to treat certain conditions where your immune system attacks your own body, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and ulcerative colitis. It helps reduce pain, swelling, and stiffness in your joints. It can also help prevent further joint damage over time.
how_it_works: Your immune system makes a protein called TNF-alpha, which causes inflammation and damage in conditions like arthritis. Golimumab is a special lab-made antibody that finds and blocks this protein, like a key fitting into a lock. By blocking TNF-alpha, it calms down the overactive immune response so you feel better and your joints are protected.
common_side_effects: Upper respiratory infections like a stuffy or runny nose, injection site reactions such as redness or mild pain where the shot is given, sore throat, and headache. Some people may also notice mild nausea or dizziness.
warnings: Because this medicine lowers part of your immune system, you are more likely to get serious infections, including tuberculosis (TB). Your doctor will test you for TB before you start. Tell your doctor right away if you get a fever, chills, or feel unusually sick. It may also increase the risk of certain cancers. Do not use it if you have a serious active infection. Tell your doctor about all vaccines you need, as some live vaccines should be avoided while taking this medicine.
typical_dosing: Golimumab is usually given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous) once a month at home using a prefilled pen or syringe. For some conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, it may be given as an IV infusion at a clinic every 8 weeks after starting doses. Your doctor will decide the right dose and schedule for your specific condition.
